subject: Science
board: National Curriculum KS3 (aligned to AQA GCSE progression)
source: Drive: Schemes of work Science 'Science - Y7 - Autumn 1 - Termly Plan' and 'science KS3 SOW' (cells, particle theory, Earth and rocks, respiration), Biology/Chemistry/Physics 5yr SoW; National Curriculum KS3 Science

lessons.title: Animal and plant cells
objectives: Describe the structure of animal and plant cells
State the function of the nucleus, cell membrane, cytoplasm, cell wall, chloroplasts and vacuole
Identify differences between plant and animal cells

keywords.def: the basic unit of all living organisms
contains genetic material and controls the cell's activities
controls what enters and leaves the cell
contains chlorophyll and is where photosynthesis happens
a rigid layer of cellulose that supports plant cells

starter: Bismillah. Name three characteristics of living things.
What is the smallest part of a living thing that you can think of?
Why can't we see cells with our eyes alone?

teach.heading: Cells: the building blocks of life
bullets: All living things are made of cells
Most cells are too small to see
We use microscopes to see them
teach.note: Robert Hooke first used the word 'cell' in 1665 after looking at cork. Ask: how many cells do you think are in the human body? (Around 30 trillion.) Link to Qur'an 2:164 as an invitation to reflect on the signs of creation, without claiming the verse mentions cells.

teach.heading: Animal cell structure
bullets: Cell membrane: controls entry and exit
teach.note: Show a labelled diagram. Mitochondria are where aerobic respiration happens (preview of later lesson). Misconception: the nucleus is the 'brain' that thinks; say 'control centre' that holds genetic instructions.

teach.heading: Plant cell structure
bullets: Cell wall: strong, made of cellulose
teach.note: Plant cells are often brick-shaped. Chloroplasts contain chlorophyll, which absorbs light. Not all plant cells have chloroplasts (root cells do not, because they are underground).

teach.heading: Comparing the two
teach.note: Build a Venn diagram live. Ask why animals do not need a cell wall or chloroplasts.

teach.heading: Seeing cells
bullets: Light microscopes magnify up to about 1500 times
teach.note: Practical demonstration safe online: we do not handle stains or sharp tools at home. Show a teacher-recorded video or virtual microscope of onion epidermis (stained with iodine) and cheek cells (methylene blue). Pupils may draw from the video. Children could also look at a photo of onion skin.

practice: Which part of the cell controls what enters and leaves?
Name two structures found in plant cells but not animal cells.
Why do root cells not contain chloroplasts?
independent: Draw and label a plant cell and an animal cell using the words nucleus, cytoplasm, cell membrane, mitochondria, cell wall, chloroplast and vacuole.
Create a table of structure, function and found in (plant, animal or both).
Write three sentences comparing plant and animal cells.
exit: What is the function of the nucleus?
Name one structure only found in plant cells and say what it does.
lessons.homework: Make a model of a plant cell or animal cell using household items and label each part.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: provide labelled diagrams and a colour-coded keyword mat. Stretch: explain why a leaf cell has many chloroplasts but a root cell has none.

lessons.unit: Chemistry: Particles and states of matter
lessons.title: Solids, liquids and gases
objectives: Describe the properties of solids, liquids and gases
Classify materials into the three states of matter
Explain why some materials are hard to classify

keywords.def: fixed shape and volume, cannot be compressed
fixed volume, takes the shape of its container, flows
no fixed shape or volume, fills its container, easily compressed
to squeeze into a smaller volume

starter: Bismillah. Name the three states of matter.
Is a sponge a solid, liquid or gas? Argue your case.
Name a gas that you cannot see but breathe every day.

teach.heading: Matter
bullets: Matter is anything with mass and volume
teach.note: Define matter. Light and sound are not matter. Ask 'Is air matter?' Show that a balloon has mass when inflated (video) or squeeze a sealed syringe.

teach.heading: Properties of solids
teach.note: Misconception: powders flow so are liquids. Each grain is a solid; the powder pours because grains slide past each other.

teach.heading: Properties of liquids
bullets: Take the shape of the container
teach.note: Safe demo at home: pour 100 ml of water between different cups, volume remains the same.

teach.heading: Properties of gases
teach.note: Safe demo: a sealed plastic syringe or a sealed bag of air squashes easily, but a bag of water does not. Link to bicycle pumps.

teach.heading: Comparison table
teach.note: Build the table together. Discuss tricky materials: toothpaste, foam, jelly. Encourage justification rather than one right answer.

practice: Classify: oxygen, olive oil, copper, steam, honey, salt.
Why can a gas be compressed but a liquid cannot?
Explain why sand can be poured but is still a solid.
independent: Complete a table comparing shape, volume, ability to flow and compressibility for solids, liquids and gases.
Write a paragraph explaining how you decide if a material is a solid, liquid or gas.
Give two examples of materials that are hard to classify and explain why.
exit: Which state of matter has no fixed shape or volume?
Why is a gas easy to compress?
lessons.homework: Find 12 materials around your home and classify them as solid, liquid or gas, with a reason for any tricky ones.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: provide sorting cards with images and key terms. Stretch: explain gels and foams in terms of states of matter.

lessons.title: The structure of the Earth
objectives: Describe the layers of the Earth: crust, mantle, outer core and inner core
Compare the properties and temperatures of the layers
Explain how scientists know about the inside of the Earth

keywords.def: the thin, solid outer layer of the Earth
the thick, hot layer of semi-solid rock beneath the crust
the centre of the Earth, made mainly of iron and nickel
vibrations from earthquakes that travel through the Earth

starter: Bismillah. How deep do you think the deepest mine or hole is?
Name the three states of matter.
What is the Earth made from?

teach.heading: Four layers
teach.note: Compare to an egg or a peach. Radius of the Earth is about 6400 km. The deepest borehole is only about 12 km, so most of what we know is indirect.

teach.heading: The crust
teach.note: Oceanic crust is thinner (about 5 to 10 km) and denser; continental crust is thicker (about 30 to 70 km). The crust is like the skin of an apple, relatively.

teach.heading: Mantle and core
bullets: Mantle: about 2900 km thick, flows slowly
Outer core: liquid iron and nickel
teach.note: The inner core is solid because of the immense pressure although it is as hot as the Sun's surface (about 5000 to 6000 degrees Celsius). The mantle is solid rock that flows very slowly over millions of years.

teach.heading: How do we know?
bullets: Some waves cannot pass through liquid
teach.note: S-waves cannot travel through liquids, which is how scientists discovered the liquid outer core. Keep it at KS3 level.

teach.heading: Model it
teach.note: Safe activity: make a model with 4 colours of playdough or layers of fruit/food. Do not use knives unsupervised. Draw to scale on paper with a 6.4 cm radius circle (1 cm = 1000 km).

practice: Put the Earth's layers in order from the surface.
Why is the inner core solid even though it is hotter than the outer core?
How do seismic waves help us study the Earth?
independent: Draw a labelled cross-section of the Earth with the thickness of each layer.
Complete a table: layer, state, approximate thickness, composition.
Explain how we know the outer core is liquid.
exit: Name the four layers of the Earth.
Which layer do we live on?
lessons.homework: Draw a scale model of the Earth's layers and write one fact about each.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: provide a diagram with a word bank. Stretch: explain why the oceanic crust sinks beneath continental crust.

lessons.title: Unicellular and multicellular organisms
objectives: Distinguish unicellular from multicellular organisms
Describe examples such as amoeba and yeast
Explain the advantages of being multicellular

keywords.def: an organism made of one cell
an organism made of many cells
a living thing
an organism too small to see without a microscope

starter: Bismillah. Name two structures in an animal cell.
How many cells do you think a human has?
Is a bacterium alive? Why?

teach.heading: One cell or many?
bullets: Humans, plants and fungi like mushrooms are multicellular
teach.note: Ask for examples. Misconception: unicellular organisms are simple or primitive. One cell must carry out all seven life processes.

teach.heading: Amoeba
bullets: Changes shape to move and feed
teach.note: Amoeba surrounds food and engulfs it. Show a video. The cell contains a nucleus and cytoplasm; there is no cell wall.

teach.heading: Yeast
teach.note: Link to bread. Baker's yeast makes carbon dioxide, which makes dough rise (preview of anaerobic respiration). Brewing is not relevant to our context; focus on baking.

teach.heading: Why be multicellular?
teach.note: Specialisation is the key idea. A large organism cannot rely on diffusion alone because the surface area to volume ratio falls (GCSE link). Do not overload.

teach.heading: Looking at pond life
teach.note: Safe online practical: show a video of pond water under a microscope. At home children should not collect pond water. Handwashing is important after any contact with water outdoors.

practice: Classify: amoeba, oak tree, yeast, camel, bacterium.
State one advantage of being multicellular.
How does an amoeba obtain food?
independent: Create a table comparing unicellular and multicellular organisms with three examples each.
Write a paragraph: Why can multicellular organisms grow larger than unicellular ones?
Draw and label an amoeba and describe how it moves and feeds.
exit: Name one unicellular organism.
What is an advantage of having specialised cells?
lessons.homework: Research one unicellular organism and write five facts about it.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: provide a sorting activity with pictures. Stretch: explain why a unicellular organism is limited in size.

lessons.unit: Chemistry: Particles and states of matter
lessons.title: The particle model
objectives: Describe the arrangement and movement of particles in solids, liquids and gases
Use the particle model to explain the properties of each state
Evaluate the limitations of particle diagrams

keywords.def: a tiny piece of matter: an atom or molecule
the energy an object has because it is moving
to move rapidly back and forth in place
a simplified way of representing an idea

starter: Bismillah. List two properties of a gas.
Why can't a solid be poured?
What does the word 'model' mean in science?

teach.heading: Everything is made of particles
bullets: Matter is made of tiny particles
Particles are too small to see
teach.note: Hook: a drop of food colouring spreads in water because particles are moving. Do not call particles 'atoms' only; they may be atoms, molecules or ions.

teach.heading: Solid particles
teach.note: Draw a lattice. Explain fixed shape and volume because particles are held in place. Strong forces of attraction between particles.

teach.heading: Liquid particles
teach.note: Liquids flow because particles slide over each other. They keep their volume because particles stay close.

teach.heading: Gas particles
teach.note: Gases fill containers because particles move freely. They compress because there is lots of space. Misconception: gas particles are tiny and the space between is 'air'; the space is empty.

teach.heading: Limits of the model
bullets: Particles are drawn as solid spheres
teach.note: Evaluate the model: what does it show well, and what can't it show? A good link to what a scientific model is. Safe activity: pupils act as particles, moving in their space with controlled movement.

practice: Describe how particles are arranged in a liquid.
Why can a gas be compressed but a solid cannot?
Draw particle diagrams for a solid, a liquid and a gas.
independent: Create a table of the three states with arrangement, movement, forces and an everyday example.
Explain why a solid has a fixed shape using the particle model.
Write a paragraph explaining why a model can be useful but also have limitations.
exit: How are particles arranged in a gas?
Why does a liquid take the shape of its container?
lessons.homework: Draw cartoon-style particle diagrams of ice, water and steam and write two sentences about each.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: use physical modelling and sentence starters. Stretch: explain why the particles in ice vibrate less than those in water.

lessons.title: Tectonic plates
objectives: Explain that the Earth's crust is split into tectonic plates
Describe what happens at plate boundaries
Link plate movement to earthquakes and volcanoes

keywords.def: a large slab of the Earth's crust and upper mantle
where two tectonic plates meet
shaking of the ground caused by sudden movement in the crust
an opening where molten rock reaches the surface

starter: Bismillah. Name the layers of the Earth.
What causes an earthquake?
Have you seen a world map? What do you notice about South America and Africa?

teach.heading: Plates on the move
bullets: The crust is cracked into plates
They move a few centimetres a year
teach.note: About as fast as fingernails grow. Convection currents in the mantle help drive movement. Keep it at a basic level for KS3.

teach.heading: Evidence: Wegener
teach.note: Alfred Wegener proposed continental drift in 1912. It was rejected at first because he could not explain how the continents moved. Good link to how science changes with evidence.

teach.heading: Plate boundaries
teach.note: Use a diagram. Example: Himalayas formed where Indian and Eurasian plates collide. The San Andreas fault is a sliding boundary.

teach.heading: Earthquakes and volcanoes
teach.note: Safe demo: push two hands together on a table covered with a cloth or sand to show crumpling or use a video. Do not use anything that can cause injury. Discuss compassion for those affected by disasters and the Islamic duty to help (sadaqah).

teach.heading: Staying safe
teach.note: Earthquakes cannot be predicted accurately; volcanoes can sometimes be monitored. Discuss how countries prepare.

practice: What are tectonic plates?
Which type of boundary forms mountains?
Give two pieces of evidence for continental drift.
independent: Label a world map with the main tectonic plates (use a provided outline) and mark one earthquake zone.
Draw three plate boundary diagrams with arrows showing the movement.
Write a paragraph explaining why Wegener's idea was not accepted at first.
exit: What causes an earthquake?
Name one piece of evidence for moving continents.
lessons.homework: Research a recent earthquake or volcanic eruption and write five facts.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: provide labelled diagrams and a word bank. Stretch: explain why the Atlantic Ocean is getting wider.

lessons.title: Specialised cells, tissues, organs and systems
objectives: Describe how specialised cells are adapted to their functions
Order the levels of organisation from cell to organism
Give examples of tissues, organs and organ systems

keywords.def: a cell with a special shape or structure for its job
a group of similar cells working together
a group of different tissues working together
a group of organs working together

starter: Bismillah. Name one advantage of being multicellular.
Name three organs in your body.
What does 'adapted' mean?

teach.heading: Specialised cells
bullets: Examples: red blood cell, root hair cell
teach.note: Red blood cells: no nucleus, biconcave to carry more oxygen. Root hair cells: long projection, large surface area to absorb water. Nerve cells: long to carry signals.

teach.heading: More specialised cells
teach.note: Muscle cells contain many mitochondria for energy. Ciliated cells line the windpipe and sweep mucus and dust away from the lungs. Palisade cells are in the top of leaves.

teach.heading: Levels of organisation
teach.note: Use the example: muscle cell, muscular tissue, stomach, digestive system. Pupils say it aloud in order: 'cells make tissues, tissues make organs'.

teach.heading: Examples of organ systems
teach.note: Ask which organs are in each system. Misconception: the heart is an organ system, when it is an organ in the circulatory system.

teach.heading: Plants have levels too
bullets: Roots, stems and leaves form a system
teach.note: Plant organisation: cells, tissues, organs (leaf), organ systems (shoot system and root system).

practice: Why does a red blood cell have no nucleus?
Put in order: tissue, organ, cell, organ system.
Name the organs in the digestive system that you know.
independent: Draw and label three specialised cells and explain how each is adapted.
Match each organ to its organ system: heart, stomach, lungs, brain, kidney.
Write a short explanation of how cells, tissues, organs and systems work together to digest food.
exit: What is a tissue?
How is a root hair cell adapted to absorb water?
lessons.homework: Create a poster showing the levels of organisation for the circulatory system.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: provide labelled cells and a matching exercise. Stretch: explain why a nerve cell is very long.

lessons.unit: Chemistry: Particles and states of matter
lessons.title: Gas pressure and diffusion
objectives: Explain gas pressure using the particle model
Explain how temperature affects gas pressure
Describe diffusion in gases and liquids

keywords.def: the force of gas particles colliding with a surface
the spreading of particles from high to low concentration
the amount of a substance in a given volume
movement in unpredictable directions

starter: Bismillah. How are the particles arranged in a gas?
Why can a gas be squashed?
How does the smell of cooking reach you from another room?

teach.heading: Pressure in a gas
teach.note: Link to a tyre or a balloon. A balloon expands because gas pressure pushes outwards on the rubber.

teach.heading: Temperature and pressure
bullets: They hit the walls harder and more often
teach.note: Misconception: particles expand when heated. They move faster and spread out, but each particle stays the same size. Safe demo: show a video of a sealed can or syringe being warmed.

teach.heading: Diffusion in gases
bullets: Particles spread out from high to low concentration
teach.note: Safe demo at home: spray air freshener or open a fruit in a room and time when each pupil smells it. Record the time. Check for allergies and use a very small amount.

teach.heading: Diffusion in liquids
teach.note: Safe demo: one drop of food colouring in cold water and one in warm (not boiling; warm tap water; adult supervises). Time how long until evenly mixed.

teach.heading: Explaining with particles
teach.note: Practise a full explanation: 'The perfume particles move randomly. There are more particles near the bottle, so more move away than towards it, so they spread out.'

practice: Explain why a balloon bursts if it is heated too much.
Why does diffusion happen faster in warm water?
Which has the higher concentration of perfume: near the bottle or at the other side of the room?
independent: Explain gas pressure using particles and collisions, with a diagram.
Record and graph results of the food colouring diffusion test, if you carried it out.
Write a paragraph explaining why a smell from the kitchen spreads through the house.
exit: Define diffusion.
What happens to gas pressure when a gas is heated in a sealed container?
lessons.homework: Explain three examples of diffusion in everyday life using particle ideas.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: provide a diagram frame with sentence starters. Stretch: explain what happens to pressure if the volume of a gas is halved.

lessons.title: Igneous, sedimentary and metamorphic rocks
objectives: Describe how igneous, sedimentary and metamorphic rocks form
Identify features of each rock type
Link rock properties to uses

keywords.def: rock formed when molten rock cools and solidifies
rock formed from compressed layers of sediment
rock changed by heat and pressure
the preserved remains or traces of a living thing in rock

starter: Bismillah. Name the layers of the Earth.
What happens to lava when it cools?
Name one rock you have seen.

teach.heading: Three rock families
teach.note: Introduce each name's meaning: igneous from the Latin for fire, sedimentary from sediment, metamorphic from change of form.

teach.heading: Igneous rocks
bullets: Form from cooled magma or lava
teach.note: Granite cools slowly underground; basalt cools quickly at the surface. Crystal size depends on cooling rate. Ask why.

teach.heading: Sedimentary rocks
teach.note: Sediments are laid down in layers, compressed and cemented over millions of years. Limestone often comes from the shells of sea creatures. Fossils form only in sedimentary rock.

teach.heading: Metamorphic rocks
bullets: Existing rock changed by heat and pressure
teach.note: Limestone becomes marble; shale becomes slate. Misconception: metamorphic rocks melt. If they melt, they would become igneous.

teach.heading: Uses of rock
teach.note: Link properties to uses.

practice: How does granite form and why does it have large crystals?
Which rock type contains fossils?
Name the rock type that marble is.
independent: Create a table of rock type, how it forms, key features and examples.
Explain why basalt has smaller crystals than granite.
Write about a use of each rock type.
exit: Which rock type forms from cooled lava?
How is metamorphic rock formed?
lessons.homework: Find three rock types in buildings or objects around you and identify which family they belong to.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: provide labelled photographs and a table. Stretch: explain why fossils are not found in igneous rocks.

lessons.title: Diffusion in living things
objectives: Describe diffusion in terms of particles in living systems
Give examples of diffusion in the body and in plants
Explain how surface area and concentration gradient affect the rate of diffusion

keywords.def: net movement of particles from a high to a low concentration
the difference in concentration between two areas
the total area of an object's surface
lets some substances through but not others

starter: Bismillah. Define diffusion.
Why does a smell spread more quickly in a warm room?
What gas do we breathe in and what gas do we breathe out?

teach.heading: Diffusion into cells
bullets: Oxygen diffuses in; carbon dioxide diffuses out
teach.note: Cells use oxygen for respiration and produce carbon dioxide. The membrane is like a security gate: small particles pass, large molecules cannot.

teach.heading: Examples in the body
bullets: Oxygen moves from lungs to blood
teach.note: Link to the lungs and small intestine. Alveoli are covered in preview only. Keep to a basic level.

teach.heading: Concentration gradient
bullets: No energy needed from the cell
teach.note: Draw a diagram with many dots on one side, few on the other. Say 'from high to low concentration'; avoid 'to where there is more room'.

teach.heading: Surface area
bullets: Single-celled organisms have a large surface area to volume
teach.note: Cut a cube into smaller cubes to show surface area increases. Safe practical: cut sugar lumps or draw cubes on paper. The small intestine and root hair cells are adapted.

teach.heading: Investigating diffusion
bullets: Place a tea bag in warm and cold water
teach.note: Safe at-home practical with warm tap water only. Variables: temperature (change), time (measure), volume of water (same). Record in a table.

practice: What does 'partially permeable' mean?
Why do cells in the small intestine have folded surfaces?
Describe the direction of diffusion of oxygen into a cell.
independent: Draw and label a diagram of oxygen diffusing from the lung to the blood.
Explain how surface area affects the rate of diffusion.
Write a conclusion for the food colouring investigation, using ideas about particles and concentration.
exit: Define concentration gradient.
Name one substance that diffuses out of cells.
lessons.homework: Explain how diffusion helps a single-celled organism get oxygen.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: provide a diagram with arrows to label. Stretch: explain why a bigger concentration difference speeds up diffusion.

lessons.unit: Chemistry: Particles and states of matter
lessons.title: Changes of state
objectives: Name the changes of state: melting, freezing, boiling, evaporating, condensing and subliming
Explain changes of state in terms of particles and energy
Distinguish between evaporation and boiling

keywords.def: the temperature at which a solid becomes a liquid
the temperature at which a liquid boils into a gas
a solid changing directly to a gas
a change that is reversible and makes no new substance

starter: Bismillah. Draw particles in a liquid.
What happens to ice on a hot day?
Is melting reversible?

teach.heading: Six changes
bullets: Boiling and evaporating: liquid to gas
teach.note: Also condensing (gas to liquid) and subliming (solid to gas) such as dry ice or iodine. Show a diagram with arrows.

teach.heading: Adding energy
teach.note: Particles themselves do not change; only their arrangement and energy. Misconception: the particles melt or get bigger.

teach.heading: Removing energy
teach.note: Link to condensation on a cold glass. The change is reversible, so it is a physical change.

teach.heading: Evaporation versus boiling
bullets: Evaporation: at the surface, any temperature
Boiling: throughout the liquid, at the boiling point
Bubbles of vapour form when boiling
teach.note: Safe demo: puddle drying or wet cloth for evaporation; video of a boiling kettle or pan for boiling. Pupils must not handle boiling water.

teach.heading: Melting and boiling points
teach.note: Use a table of data: oxygen boils at about -183 °C, iron melts at about 1538 °C. Ask pupils to classify a substance at a given temperature.

practice: Name the change from gas to liquid.
At 25 °C, is water a solid, liquid or gas? And at 120 °C?
Explain melting using the particle model.
independent: Draw a state-change diagram with all six changes and arrows.
Use a table of melting and boiling points to say the state of five substances at 20 °C.
Explain the differences between evaporation and boiling.
exit: What is sublimation?
What happens to particles when a solid melts?
lessons.homework: Explain, using particles, why a wet cloth dries faster on a hot, windy day.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: provide a labelled state-change diagram. Stretch: explain why a puddle dries even if the temperature is below 100 °C.

lessons.title: Minerals and rock properties
objectives: Explain that rocks are made from minerals
Describe how to test rock properties such as hardness and permeability
Relate rock properties to their uses

keywords.def: a naturally occurring solid with a definite chemical composition
allows liquids to pass through
how resistant a material is to scratching
a solid whose particles are arranged in a regular pattern

starter: Bismillah. Name the three rock families.
Which rock family contains fossils?
Why might a builder choose granite for a worktop?

teach.heading: Rocks and minerals
bullets: A mineral has a regular structure
teach.note: Ask: is granite a single substance? No, it is a mixture. Quartz is silicon dioxide.

teach.heading: Hardness
bullets: A harder mineral scratches a softer one
teach.note: Safe at home: test with a fingernail, a copper coin (about 3.5) and a steel nail (about 5.5) on household soap or chalk. Use caution with nails and keep hands away from the blade end.

teach.heading: Permeability
teach.note: Safe at-home test: drop water on a piece of brick or a stone and watch it soak in. Connect to groundwater and aquifers.

teach.heading: Properties and uses
bullets: Soft rocks are easy to carve
teach.note: Ask pupils to choose a rock for a roof and explain with properties. Tie to crafts of Islamic architecture such as carved stone or marble, in general terms.

teach.heading: Crystals
teach.note: Safe at-home practical: dissolve salt or sugar in warm water, leave on a saucer to form crystals. Do not taste. Warm tap water only and an adult present.

practice: Is granite one mineral or a mixture?
A rock scratches the copper coin but not the steel nail. Estimate its hardness.
Which property would you test to find out if a rock can hold water in a reservoir?
independent: Make a table of three rocks with hardness, permeability and a use.
Explain how crystal size shows how fast a rock cooled.
Write a short report on a property test of a household stone or brick.
exit: What is a mineral?
Name a property you can test for rocks.
lessons.homework: Do a hardness test on three household items using a fingernail and a coin and record your results.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: provide a table of results to complete. Stretch: explain why diamonds can cut glass.

lessons.title: Aerobic respiration
objectives: State that respiration releases energy from food
Write the word and symbol equations for aerobic respiration
Describe where respiration takes place

keywords.def: a chemical reaction in cells that releases energy from glucose
needing oxygen
a sugar used as a fuel by cells
parts of a cell where aerobic respiration happens

starter: Bismillah. Why do we need food?
Where is the energy in food stored?
What is the difference between breathing and respiration?

teach.heading: Respiration is not breathing
bullets: Breathing moves air in and out
It happens in every living cell
teach.note: Common misconception: plants do not respire. They respire all the time, day and night. Link to the energy in food from digestion lessons.

teach.heading: Aerobic respiration equation
teach.note: Write the word equation first, then the symbol equation, and show it is balanced: 6 C, 12 H, 18 O each side. Energy is released, not made.

teach.heading: Where it happens
bullets: Cells with high energy needs have more
teach.note: Muscle cells and liver cells have many mitochondria. Ask pupils to link to Lesson 1 cell structure.

teach.heading: Uses of energy
teach.note: Respiration releases energy for muscle contraction, keeping warm (37 °C) and building molecules. Energy is not a substance; it is transferred.

teach.heading: Observing evidence
bullets: Breathe on a cold mirror: water vapour
Lime water turns cloudy with carbon dioxide
teach.note: Safe online approach: pupils breathe onto a cold spoon to see condensation. Use a teacher video for the limewater test, as limewater is not a household item. Germinating seeds in a flask are shown on video.

practice: Write the word equation for aerobic respiration.
Count the atoms on each side of the symbol equation to show it is balanced.
Why do muscle cells have many mitochondria?
independent: Explain the difference between breathing and respiration in three sentences.
Draw a diagram of a cell showing where respiration takes place with the reactants and products.
Answer: what evidence shows that living things release carbon dioxide?
exit: Write the word equation for aerobic respiration.
In which part of the cell does aerobic respiration happen?
lessons.homework: Explain why you breathe faster during exercise, using the equation for respiration.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: provide equation cards to rearrange. Stretch: balance the equation and explain why 6 oxygen molecules are needed.

lessons.unit: Chemistry: Particles and states of matter
lessons.title: Heating and cooling curves
objectives: Interpret a heating curve and a cooling curve
Explain flat sections using particle ideas
Use melting and boiling points to identify a substance

keywords.def: a graph of temperature against time as a substance is heated
a flat part of a graph where the value does not change
energy used to change state without changing temperature
a single substance with a sharp melting point

starter: Bismillah. State the melting point of water.
What happens to the temperature of ice as it melts?
Describe the particles in a liquid.

teach.heading: A heating curve
teach.note: Draw the axes: time on x, temperature on y. Sections: solid warming, melting (flat), liquid warming, boiling (flat), gas warming.

teach.heading: Why flat sections?
teach.note: At melting, energy is used to overcome forces between particles. Misconception: the substance stops absorbing heat. It continues; the energy changes the state, not the temperature.

teach.heading: Cooling curves
bullets: Flat sections when condensing and freezing
teach.note: Mirror image of the heating curve. Flat parts happen at the same temperatures (boiling point and melting point).

teach.heading: Reading data
bullets: Find melting point from the first plateau
Find boiling point from the second
teach.note: Provide a data set for a substance: e.g. a plateau at 0 °C and another at 100 °C, so it is water. Practise reading values from graphs.

teach.heading: Doing the experiment
teach.note: Safe at-home practical: crushed ice in a cup with a kitchen thermometer, left at room temperature. Record every 2 minutes. No boiling water. Use class data or a video for the boiling stage.

practice: Describe what is happening on a flat section of a heating curve.
Read the melting point from a given graph.
Why is the cooling curve a mirror image of the heating curve?
independent: Draw and label a heating curve for water, marking the states.
Plot the data from the ice experiment on a graph.
Explain using particles why the temperature does not change while a substance is melting.
exit: What does a flat section on a heating curve show?
How can we find the boiling point from a graph?
lessons.homework: Sketch a cooling curve for steam to ice with labels for each section.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: provide a partly labelled graph. Stretch: explain what a sloping melting section would show about the sample.

lessons.title: The rock cycle
objectives: Describe the processes of the rock cycle
Explain weathering, erosion, transportation and deposition
Draw and explain a rock cycle diagram

keywords.def: the breaking down of rock in one place
the wearing away and carrying off of rock by wind, water or ice
when sediment is dropped and settles
pressing sediment together under its own weight

starter: Bismillah. Name the three rock families.
What is a sedimentary rock made from?
What happens to rock when it gets very hot?

teach.heading: Weathering
teach.note: Freeze-thaw: water gets into cracks, freezes, expands and splits the rock. Safe approach: show a video or photographs of rocks split by frost; do not freeze sealed bottles at home.

teach.heading: Erosion, transport and deposition
teach.note: Distinguish weathering (in place) from erosion (movement). Misconception: they mean the same thing. Sediment is deposited when the flow slows.

teach.heading: Making sedimentary rock
teach.note: Takes millions of years. Safe model: stack layers of dough or pressed sand/rice; press with a book.

teach.heading: Heat, pressure and melting
teach.note: Link to plate movements. The cycle never ends. Safe demo: crayon shavings in foil pressed (compaction) and warmed gently by an adult with a hairdryer (heat) to model metamorphism; or watch a video.

teach.heading: The whole cycle
teach.note: Draw the cycle on the board and ask pupils to trace different pathways. There is no single starting point. Invite pupils to reflect with humility on the vast ages over which Allah's creation has changed.

practice: What is the difference between weathering and erosion?
Which process turns loose sediment into rock?
Describe one route from igneous rock to metamorphic rock.
independent: Draw a labelled rock cycle diagram including the three rock types and all processes.
Write a story of a grain of sand through the rock cycle.
Explain why the rock cycle takes millions of years.
exit: Name two processes in the rock cycle.
How are metamorphic rocks formed?
lessons.homework: Draw a comic strip of a rock travelling through the cycle.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: provide a rock cycle diagram with missing words. Stretch: explain why igneous rock on a mountain can eventually become a sedimentary rock at sea.

lessons.title: Anaerobic respiration
objectives: Define anaerobic respiration
Compare anaerobic respiration in humans and yeast
Compare aerobic and anaerobic respiration

keywords.def: without oxygen
a substance made in muscles during anaerobic respiration
anaerobic respiration in yeast, producing ethanol and carbon dioxide
the extra oxygen needed after exercise to break down lactic acid

starter: Bismillah. Write the word equation for aerobic respiration.
What happens to your breathing during a sprint?
Where does respiration take place in a cell?

teach.heading: Respiration without oxygen
bullets: Glucose is only partly broken down
teach.note: Aerobic respiration releases many times more energy per glucose than anaerobic. Anaerobic is quick but inefficient.

teach.heading: In humans
bullets: Happens in muscles during hard exercise
teach.note: Word equation: glucose → lactic acid (+ energy). Misconception: lactic acid causes the pain the next day; it is cleared within an hour or so. Muscle soreness has other causes.

teach.heading: Recovery
teach.note: Link to heart rate and breathing recovering. Fitter people repay oxygen debt faster.

teach.heading: In yeast
teach.note: Word equation: glucose → ethanol + carbon dioxide. In bread the ethanol evaporates during baking. Alcohol production for drinks is not relevant to our context.

teach.heading: Bread-dough investigation
bullets: Mix yeast, sugar and warm water
teach.note: Safe practical at home with an adult: dried yeast, a teaspoon of sugar, warm (not hot) tap water in a clean plastic bottle with a balloon on top. Compare with a bottle with no sugar. Do not drink. Warm tap water only.

practice: Write the word equation for anaerobic respiration in humans.
Write the word equation for anaerobic respiration in yeast.
Why does anaerobic respiration release less energy?
independent: Create a table comparing aerobic and anaerobic respiration: oxygen needed, products, energy released.
Explain why bread dough rises.
Write a paragraph explaining why athletes keep breathing heavily after a sprint.
exit: What is made in muscles during anaerobic respiration?
What gas makes bread rise?
lessons.homework: Draw a mind map linking aerobic respiration, anaerobic respiration, exercise and yeast.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: provide equation cards to match. Stretch: explain why yeast in a sealed container with sugar produces gas but not when there is no sugar.
